clue.text: Lippy's extremely messy on side of face

indicators.note: on means placed against or after, so the selected letter is sent second, after the facial feature

parts.note: the fleshy side of the face below the eye

indicators.note: an extremity is an end, and here only the far end of the word is wanted

parts.note: the final letter of messy

explanation.surface: Someone with badly smeared lipstick has it all over one side of their face.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extremely' usually takes both outside letters; here it takes only the last one, which sits after the facial feature since 'on' places it next to it.
explanation.definitionFit: Lippy is British slang for impudent or answering back, which is what cheeky means.

clue.text: Aristocrat loses heart, following brief part in government

indicators.note: read as 'there follows', it sends the shortened part second, after the noble
losing its heart means the central letter of the noble's title is dropped

parts.note: a European nobleman

indicators.note: something brief is cut short, so the word loses its final letter

parts.note: an actor's part

explanation.surface: A peer quits in dismay after being given only a minor government post.
explanation.walkthrough: Strictly 'following' would put the aristocrat second; the setter reads it as 'there follows', a looseness bloggers noted at the time. 'Government' as a definition is loose too: it means directing or controlling.
explanation.definitionFit: Control is the power of directing or ruling, a sense close to government as in governing a vehicle or a nation.

clue.text: Chuck out ecstasy and cocaine found in plane

parts.note: E is slang for the drug ecstasy

indicators.note: the drug letter is found inside the aircraft word, so it sits within it

parts.note: a jet aircraft
C is slang for cocaine

explanation.surface: Drugs discovered on an aircraft get the smuggler thrown off.
explanation.definitionFit: To eject someone is to throw them out forcibly, which is what chuck out means informally.

clue.text: Relish being raised on boat

indicators.note: in a down clue, one thing on another sits above it, so the vessel comes first and the lifted word below

parts.note: a ketch is a two-masted sailing boat
something raised is up

explanation.surface: Someone enjoys the feeling of being lifted high on a sailing boat.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'on' puts the raised word beneath the boat. 'Relish' looks like a verb meaning enjoy; it is the noun for a condiment.
explanation.definitionFit: Ketchup is a tomato sauce, a kind of relish or condiment served with food.

clue.text: Sweet's twice as good in France

parts.note: bon is French for good
the French word repeated a second time

explanation.surface: A sweet that is doubly good, at least by French standards.
explanation.definitionFit: A bonbon is a sweet or confection, the name taken from French baby talk for a treat.

clue.text: Demanding single or return to America

parts.note: single means one

indicators.note: to return is to go back the way you came, so the little word is read backwards

parts.note: taken as written before being turned round
the United States

explanation.surface: A ticket clerk insists on knowing whether a traveller wants a single or a return to the States.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'single or return' as a choice of rail tickets; 'return' actually acts on the word or.
explanation.definitionFit: An onerous task is burdensome and makes heavy demands, so it is demanding.

clue.text: Army unit's rising fuel bill cut by reservists having nitrogen

indicators.note: the reservists cut into the middle of the reversed words, sitting inside them
in a down clue rising means the words read from bottom to top, back to front

parts.note: oil is a fuel
a tab is a bill, as in picking up the tab
TA is the Territorial Army, Britain's volunteer reserve
N is the chemical symbol for nitrogen

explanation.surface: An army unit complains of a fuel bill that keeps rising despite cuts.
explanation.walkthrough: TA is the Territorial Army, Britain's volunteer reserve, so 'reservists' is a standard crossword source for those two letters; the nitrogen symbol is tacked on at the very end.
explanation.definitionFit: A battalion is a large army unit of several companies, part of a regiment or brigade.

clue.text: In want of a sound pummelling!

indicators.note: sound points to how the word is spoken rather than spelt

parts.note: kneading dough is pummelling it, and it is said the same as the answer

explanation.surface: Someone who badly deserves a thorough beating.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A sound pummelling' reads as a good hiding; 'sound' is the signal that the word kneading must be heard, not seen.
explanation.definitionFit: Needing something means lacking it and requiring it, which is being in want of it.

clue.text: Puzzle's a shocker, containing central theme

indicators.note: the stun gun word holds the selected letter inside it

parts.note: a Taser is an electric stun gun

indicators.note: central asks for the middle letter of the word that follows

parts.note: the middle of the five letters of theme

explanation.surface: A puzzle whose central theme turns out to be shocking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A shocker' reads as something scandalous; it is the stun gun.
explanation.definitionFit: A teaser is a tricky problem or brain-teaser, which is a puzzle.

clue.text: With awful heat and thunder, we're not feeling well

indicators.note: something awful is in a dreadful state, so the letters are thrown into disorder

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written, apostrophe ignored

explanation.surface: In this heat and thunderstorm we all feel poorly.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a weather report, and the answer is itself a weather idiom, so the scene fits neatly.
explanation.definitionFit: Under the weather is an idiom for slightly ill or out of sorts.

clue.text: It helps the injured to walk about with companion following routine

definitions.text: It helps the injured to walk

indicators.note: following places the companion after the routine word

parts.note: C is short for circa, about
a rut is a dull fixed routine
CH is Companion of Honour, a British order

explanation.surface: A patient gets about with a friend's help after the daily routine.
explanation.walkthrough: Companion of Honour is a British order whose holders put CH after their names, which is why companion gives those two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A crutch is a support held under the arm so a person with an injured leg can walk.

clue.text: Cops raid building now and then

indicators.note: building means constructing something, so the letters are assembled into a new shape

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Police raid a building every so often.
explanation.walkthrough: 'building' looks like the place being raided; it is the signal to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Sporadic means occurring at irregular intervals, which is happening only occasionally.

clue.text: Run broken app with electronic side that catches bugs

indicators.note: a broken thing is in pieces, so the three letters are put back in another order

parts.note: to fly is to run away or flee
the three letters of app rearranged
E as in e-mail stands for electronic
R is the right side

explanation.surface: A faulty phone app exposes its electronic side to software bugs.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a description of the thing, read as 'something that catches bugs'. 'Bugs' in the surface are software faults; in the answer they are insects.
explanation.definitionFit: Flypaper is sticky paper hung up to trap flies and other insects.

clue.text: Bookmaker sees local woman, 51, before start of race

parts.note: a local is one's nearby pub
LI is 51 in Roman numerals
she refers to a woman

indicators.note: the start of a word is its opening letter only

parts.note: the first letter of race

explanation.surface: A betting-shop bookie visits a 51-year-old woman in the pub before the race starts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bookmaker' suggests a bookie taking bets; read literally it is someone who makes books. A local is British slang for one's regular pub.
explanation.definitionFit: A publisher produces and issues books, so is literally a maker of books.

clue.text: They provide support, as young birds go out

indicators.note: go out is read as an instruction for the word go to leave, so those letters are removed

parts.note: goslings are young geese
taken as written, the letters that leave

explanation.surface: Fledglings are supported as they leave the nest for the first time.
explanation.walkthrough: Starlings and nestlings tempt solvers, but only the young geese contain the two letters to remove: 'go out' tells the word go to leave.
explanation.definitionFit: Slings are hanging bands of cloth that support an injured arm, so they provide support.

clue.text: Told stories about FBI to British journalist

indicators.note: about suggests turning things around, so these three letters are moved about

parts.note: the three letters rearranged
B is the abbreviation for British
ED is short for editor, a journalist

explanation.surface: Someone spun tales about the American FBI to a British reporter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Told stories' looks like an innocent report to the press; here stories are lies.
explanation.definitionFit: To tell stories is a gentle idiom for lying, and fibbed means told small lies.

clue.text: Drive old Hillman and set off round bend

indicators.note: off means not right, so the three letters are disordered

parts.note: the Hillman Imp was a small British car of the 1960s

indicators.note: the rearranged letters go round the bend letter, enclosing it

parts.note: the letters of set rearranged
a U-bend, shaped like the letter

explanation.surface: Take an old Hillman for a spin and set off round the bend.
explanation.walkthrough: The Hillman Imp was a small British car made from 1963 to 1976. 'Drive' looks like an instruction to take the car out; it is the noun for motivation.
explanation.definitionFit: Impetus is the force or drive that keeps something moving or motivates action.

clue.text: Doddery lady pens last letter in a confused manner

indicators.note: doddery means shaky and unsteady, so these letters wobble into a new order
to pen something is to shut it in, so the rearranged letters enclose the next piece

parts.note: the four letters of lady rearranged
Z, the last letter of the alphabet, spelt out as the British say it

explanation.surface: An unsteady old lady writes out the alphabet down to Z, confusedly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pens' looks like the lady writing; it means enclosing. The British name the letter Z zed, and that spelt-out name is what goes inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Dazedly means in a stunned or bewildered way, which is a confused manner.

clue.text: Loiter behind Mum and pretend to be ill

indicators.note: behind puts the loitering word after the mother, at the back

parts.note: ma is a familiar word for mother
to linger is to loiter or hang about

explanation.surface: A child dawdles behind their mother and fakes sickness to skip school.
explanation.definitionFit: To malinger is to feign illness, usually to avoid work or duty.

clue.text: Red planet endlessly circles on pole

indicators.note: without an end, the word loses its final letter

parts.note: the red planet of the surface
two circles look like two Os
N is the north pole

explanation.surface: Mars, the red planet, keeps orbiting over the pole.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Red planet' reads as one phrase for Mars, but 'Red' is the definition and 'planet' alone gives the word to shorten. In a down clue 'on' puts the circles above the pole.
explanation.definitionFit: Maroon is a dark brownish-red colour, so it is a shade of red.

clue.text: Projection gets everything heard by listener

parts.note: a lug is a projecting handle or ear

indicators.note: heard means we take the spoken form of the word for everything

parts.note: the whole is everything, and it is said the same as an opening

explanation.surface: A projecting part picks up every sound that reaches the ear.
explanation.walkthrough: Lughole is British slang for the ear, so 'listener' is the organ that listens, not a person.
explanation.definitionFit: Lughole is colloquial British for ear, and an ear is the body's listener.

clue.text: Part of the French Antilles has charm

indicators.note: only a part of the following words is needed, a run of letters inside them

parts.note: spans the end of French and the start of Antilles

explanation.surface: A region of the French Caribbean islands is charming.
explanation.definitionFit: To charm someone is to delight or bewitch them, which is to enchant them.

clue.text: Retired salesmen take over grand hotel for drink

indicators.note: to take over is to take in, so the reversed letters hold the hotel inside
retired means withdrawn or gone back, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: reps are sales representatives
the Ritz is a famous grand hotel in London

explanation.surface: Retired salesmen buy a grand hotel to have somewhere to drink.
explanation.walkthrough: The Ritz is a famous grand hotel in London, and reps are sales representatives; 'take over' looks like a business buyout but means take in.
explanation.definitionFit: A spritzer is a drink of white wine mixed with soda water.

clue.text: Look good with old weapon

parts.note: G is the abbreviation for good
a lance was a long spear used by mounted knights

explanation.surface: An antique weapon in fine condition.
explanation.definitionFit: A glance is a brief look, so the noun look can stand for it.

clue.text: Flooded by a fenland estuary

parts.note: taken as written
the Wash is the bay and estuary on the edge of the East Anglian Fens

explanation.surface: Low-lying land flooded by a tidal estuary in the Fens.
explanation.walkthrough: The Fens are flat marshy lowlands of eastern England, and the Wash is the large estuary they drain into.
explanation.definitionFit: Awash means covered or flooded with water.

clue.text: When capital protection falls off, it's sudden

definitions.text: When capital protection falls off, it's sudden

parts.words: When capital protection falls off, it's sudden
parts.note: surface reading: something abrupt happens when a city's defences collapse
setter's reading: capital means head, so the protection is headgear, and its tumbling marks an instant start, as with a starting signal

explanation.surface: A capital city's defences collapse suddenly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Capital' looks like a city; it is the head, as in capital punishment. Races were once started by dropping a hat, so the phrase means instantly.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means immediately, without hesitation, from the old practice of starting a contest when a hat was dropped.

clue.text: Time to fish on board ship that drifts

indicators.note: something on board a vessel is inside it, so these letters go within the ship

parts.note: SS stands for steamship
T is the abbreviation for time
a ray is a flat fish

explanation.surface: There is time to go fishing aboard a ship that is drifting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ship that drifts' reads as a drifting boat, but the definition is just 'drifts', a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To stray is to wander off course, so strays means drifts.

clue.text: Do the shakes follow the initial rash and burning?

indicators.note: shaking something jumbles it, so these letters are tossed into a new order
the initial means the opening letter of the word that follows

parts.note: the first letter of rash
the five letters of do and the rearranged

explanation.surface: Do the shakes come after the first sign of a rash and a fever?
explanation.walkthrough: 'the shakes' reads as a fever symptom; 'shakes' alone is the signal to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Red-hot means extremely hot, glowing with heat, so burning in a literal sense.
